scenes.headline: How BM25 ranks documents without learning anything
scenes.sub: A 1990s ranking function that is still the default in Lucene and Elasticsearch.
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Tofu! BM25 is a ranking function from the early nineties, and it's probably still what your search bar runs. Here's how it works.

scenes.label: The idea
scenes.text: BM25 is TF-IDF with two honest fixes: repeated words saturate instead of counting forever, and long documents are discounted.
scenes.say: It's TF-IDF with two honest fixes. Repeated words saturate instead of counting forever, and long documents get discounted.

left.title: TF-IDF
items: A long document wins by being long
left.say: Plain TF-IDF grows forever: forty mentions score forty times one. And a long document racks up counts just by being long.

right.title: BM25
items: Term frequency saturates after a few mentions
Length is normalized against the average
right.say: BM25 lets repetition saturate, and scales each count by the document's length against the average.

scenes.title: The score, one query term at a time
scenes.say: Sum this over the query terms a document contains.

parts.note: rarity: common words count almost nothing
parts.say: IDF is rarity. A word in every document, like the, counts almost nothing, so no stopword list is needed.
f is the term count, and k one makes it saturate: the first mention counts most. The default k one is one point two.
This compares the document's length to the average. The knob b, default zero point seven five, sets how hard long documents are discounted.

scenes.title: Scoring at scale: the inverted index

steps.say: In practice, an inverted index maps each term to the list of documents that contain it.
So only documents sharing a query term get scored, never the whole corpus.
Each gets the formula, and the list is sorted. No GPU, no training: it scales on commodity hardware.

scenes.text: A model doesn't have to learn anything to encode real knowledge: rarity matters, repetition saturates, length dilutes.
scenes.mark: rarity matters, repetition saturates, length dilutes

recap: Score = rarity x saturated, length-normalized count
An inverted index keeps it fast
scenes.say: To recap: rare terms dominate, repetition saturates, long documents are discounted, and an index keeps it fast.
